items.prose: A fair die has not shown a 6 in its last 20 rolls.
items.question: What is the chance the next roll is a 6?

options.why: You expected the die to make up for the missing 6s. Rolls are independent, so the drought changes nothing.
We know the die is fair. Its chance of a 6 does not drift with a streak.

feedback.correct: Every roll of a fair die is a fresh one in six.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask whether the die can remember the last 20 rolls.

explain.text: Rolls are independent, so $P(6 \mid \text{no 6 in 20}) = P(6) = \tfrac{1}{6}$. Long-run shares settle by dilution, not by the die paying back its 6s.

items.prose: A surveillance system flags 1 in 1,000 honest trades by mistake, and always flags fraud. Of 50,001 trades today, exactly one was fraudulent.
items.question: A trade is flagged. What is the chance it is the fraudulent one?

widget.label: Chance a flagged trade is fraud

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the honest trades flagged by mistake, then add the fraud.

byKey.swap: You read 1 in 1,000 as the chance a flag is wrong. It is $P(\text{flag} \mid \text{honest})$; about 50 honest trades are flagged.
byKey.thousandth: That is the false-flag rate itself. Count how many flags there are in all.

explain.text: $50{,}000 \times \tfrac{1}{1000} = 50$ honest trades are flagged, plus the fraud: 51 flags. So $P(\text{fraud} \mid \text{flag}) = \tfrac{1}{51} \approx 0.02$. A low false-flag rate on a huge pool still swamps one true case.

items.prose: A strategy won 40 of its 50 trades in 2024 and 75 of its 150 trades in 2025.
items.question: What is its win rate over both years?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the wins and the trades across both years.

byKey.plain: You averaged 0.8 and 0.5 equally. 2025 holds three times as many trades.

explain.text: $\tfrac{40 + 75}{50 + 150} = 0.575$, the weighted average $0.25 \times 0.8 + 0.75 \times 0.5$. The year with more trades pulls the overall rate towards its own.

items.prose: Of 20 funds that launched together, 12 are still open and averaged 6% a year. The 8 that closed averaged −4% a year.
items.question: What was the average return of all 20 funds, in % a year?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Weight each group by its share of the 20 funds.

byKey.open: That is the survivors’ average. Put the 8 closed funds back.
byKey.plain: You averaged 6 and −4 equally. The groups hold 12 and 8 funds.

explain.text: $\tfrac{12 \times 6 + 8 \times (-4)}{20} = \tfrac{72 - 32}{20} = 2$% a year. The open funds overstate by 4 points.

items.prose: In a falling market only 30% of days are up days. A signal flashes before 60% of up days and 30% of down days. It flashes today.
items.question: What is the chance today is an up day?

feedback.correct: Odds of 6 to 7: still below a half.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the prior odds by the likelihood ratio, then convert.

byKey.hit: You took the detection rate as the probability of an up day. Start from the 30% base rate.
byKey.odds: That is the posterior odds. Turn it into a probability: $\tfrac{6/7}{1 + 6/7}$.

explain.text: Prior odds $\tfrac{0.3}{0.7} = \tfrac{3}{7}$, likelihood ratio $\tfrac{0.6}{0.3} = 2$, posterior odds $\tfrac{6}{7}$. So $p = \tfrac{6}{13} \approx 0.46$. A good signal on a low base rate still leaves a down day more likely.

items.prose: A bet wins with chance 0.45 and pays even money. You stake £1, double after each loss, and stop at the first win or after three losses in a row.
items.question: What is the expected profit of one round, in pounds?

feedback.correct: Doubling cannot turn a losing bet into a winning one.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Weight the £1 win and the £7 loss by their chances.

byKey.one: You counted only the usual outcome. Three losses in a row cost £7 and happen with chance $0.55^3$.
byKey.zero: Zero is the answer for a fair bet. Here each bet wins only 45% of the time.
byKey.p-win: That is the expected win alone. Subtract $0.55^3 \times £7$.

explain.text: Three losses have chance $0.55^3 = 0.166375$ and cost $1 + 2 + 4 = 7$ pounds. So $E = 0.833625 - 7 \times 0.166375 = -0.331$. Each bet loses 10p per £1 staked on average, and doubling only stakes more.

items.prose: Model A makes fewer forecasting errors than model B on large-cap stocks, and fewer on small-cap stocks. Yet over all its forecasts, A makes errors more often.
items.question: What must be true?

options.text: A’s forecasts were weighted more towards the group where errors are common
There is an arithmetic mistake: this cannot happen
options.why: It can: an overall rate is a weighted average, and the two models use different weights.

options.text: A made more forecasts in total
options.why: The total count does not matter. What matters is the split between the two groups.

options.text: A is really the worse model
options.why: A beats B within both groups. Like for like, A is better.

feedback.correct: Different mixes reverse the overall comparison.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think of each overall rate as a weighted average of two group rates.

explain.text: Each overall error rate is a weighted average of the two group rates. If A forecast mostly in the harder group, its average sits near that group’s high error rate. That is Simpson’s paradox.

items.prose: A backtest reports $p = 0.02$ for a new strategy.
items.question: Which statement is correct?

options.text: If the strategy had no edge, a result this good would turn up about 2% of the time
There is a 2% chance the strategy has no edge
options.why: That swaps the condition. The p-value is $P(\text{result} \mid \text{no edge})$, not $P(\text{no edge} \mid \text{result})$.

options.text: There is a 98% chance the strategy has an edge
options.why: That is the same swap. The chance of an edge needs the prior share of real edges among strategies tried.

options.text: The strategy will beat the market 98% of the time
options.why: The p-value says nothing about how often the strategy wins.

feedback.correct: A p-value conditions on there being no edge.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what the p-value conditions on.

explain.text: $p = P(\text{a result this good} \mid \text{no edge}) = 0.02$. The chance of no edge given the result depends on how many strategies were tried and how rare real edges are. Reading one as the other is the prosecutor’s fallacy.
